reading.rtitle: Why Real Lawyers Still Watch Suits
paras: Ask a room of corporate lawyers what they think of Suits, and most of them will laugh. Set in a fictional Manhattan firm, the series follows Mike Ross, a young man hired as an associate without ever having been to law school. Armed with a photographic memory and a borrowed suit, he wins case after case, usually within a single episode. Very little of this is how the profession works, and yet the show became one of the most-watched legal dramas of its decade, finding a whole new audience on streaming platforms years after it ended.

The most obvious problem is time. Compressed into forty minutes, a dispute that would take three years in real life begins and ends before the credits roll. Real litigation is mostly paperwork: depositions taken months before any trial, thousands of documents reviewed by junior associates and paralegals, and billable hours recorded in six-minute units. Trials themselves are rare. In the United States, the vast majority of civil cases settle before they reach a jury, and most criminal cases end in a plea bargain rather than a verdict.

Then there is the courtroom itself. Television loves the surprise witness, produced at the last moment, and the cross-examination ending in a tearful confession. Lawyers objecting every thirty seconds make good television, but they would irritate any real judge. Even the closing argument, delivered by a hero walking slowly in front of the jury, is a trope borrowed from older films; in many American courts, lawyers are expected to speak from the lectern.

So why do lawyers keep watching? Partly for the pleasure of spotting the mistakes. But lawyers learning English have a better reason. Written by people who clearly listened to how lawyers talk, the dialogue is full of the language of negotiation: pressure applied politely, concessions offered at the right moment, threats that never sound like threats. Having taken its poetic license with the procedure, the show is surprisingly accurate about the one thing that matters in any deal: who needs it more. Watched with that in mind, even a far-fetched episode becomes a lesson.

listenings.text: People always ask me if my job is like television, and the honest answer is no. On television, a cross-examination is a duel. The lawyer shouts, the witness breaks down, and somebody confesses before the commercial break. In twenty years as a trial lawyer, I have never seen a confession in a courtroom. A good cross-examination is boring on purpose. I follow one rule: never ask a question you do not already know the answer to. Every question is a short step, and the witness can only say yes. And the work does not happen in the courtroom. Most of it happens months before, in depositions, in a conference room with no judge and no jury, where you find out what the witness is going to say. As for objections, I object maybe twice in a whole day. A lawyer jumping up every minute would lose the jury and annoy the judge.

Before I wrote for television, I spent four years as a paralegal at a firm in Chicago. Most of that time I was reviewing documents, thousands of them, looking for one email that somebody should never have sent. When I joined my first writers' room, the producer told me something I have never forgotten: the real work is invisible, so we cannot film it. And he was right. Nobody wants to watch a man reading in a basement. So I change the timeline. I take six months of discovery and turn it into one scene. That is poetic license, and I am comfortable with it. What I refuse to change is the way lawyers talk to each other: the politeness, the pressure, the silences. The scene I am proudest of has no courtroom at all. It is a phone call about a settlement, four minutes long, and nobody raises their voice once.

extra_audio.text: First, the client's complaint is filed in court, and the other side has a few weeks to respond. Over the next year, both sides exchange thousands of documents, reviewed line by line by associates and paralegals. Then the depositions begin: witnesses answer questions under oath in a conference room, with no judge and no jury. Six months before the trial date, with the evidence on the table, the two sides sit down to negotiate. Finally, a week before the trial, the case settles, and the courtroom scene that television promised never happens.
